url: /pavo/getting-started.md

# Getting Started

Install pavo, put a driver on `PATH`, and render a view.

## Install pavo

```sh
cargo install --git https://github.com/9aia/pavo pavo tamias-driver-config
# or, from a checkout:
cargo xtask install   # pavo + tamias-driver-config → ~/.cargo/bin
```

`tamias-driver-config` is the suite's common config API driver — it
ships with pavo so every install has at least one real driver.

## Install a view driver

Drivers are executables named `tamias-driver-<type>` found on `PATH`
or in `<tamias-home>/drivers/` (`$TAMIAS_HOME` or
`~/.local/share/tamias/drivers`). The repo ships reference drivers
under `examples/drivers/` — Python 3, stdlib only:

```sh
export PATH="$PWD/examples/drivers/demo:$PWD/examples/drivers/myco:$PWD/examples/drivers/viz-graph:$PATH"
```

Real product drivers (`tamias-driver-kuda`, `tamias-driver-myco`,
`tamias-driver-cuora`, …) install the same way — via tamias or onto
`PATH`. See [Install a driver](/how-to/install-a-driver).

## Render a view

```sh
pavo drivers                          # what pavo found
pavo views                            # every <driver>:<view> ref
pavo view demo:board                  # text summary of the tree
pavo view demo:deps --format mermaid  # graph → mermaid
pavo view demo:deps --format svg      # viz-graph renderer plugin
pavo query demo items --param status=open
```

## Open the TUI or web surface

```sh
pavo open                 # ratatui host, dashboard
pavo open demo:deps       # straight to a deep link

pavo serve --port 7420    # localhost bridge + web host
```

## Next

* [Your first view](/tutorials/first-view)
* [Architecture](/explanation/architecture)
* [CLI reference](/reference/cli)

# Your first view

This tutorial takes you from a fresh checkout to a rendered view —
using the `demo` example driver, which exercises the whole ViewNode
IR (table, kv, markdown, graph, tree) plus navbar/dashboard/statusbar
contributions.

## 1. Build and install pavo

```sh
cd pavo
cargo xtask install
```

This release-builds `pavo` and `tamias-driver-config` into
`~/.cargo/bin`.

## 2. Put the demo driver on PATH

```sh
export PATH="$PWD/examples/drivers/demo:$PATH"
pavo drivers
```

Expected output:

```
config  Config  v0.1.0  views:2  renderers:0  contributes: statusbar:1
demo  Demo  v0.1.0  views:3  renderers:0  contributes: navbar:2 dashboard:1 statusbar:1
```

`config` is the config API driver that installed with pavo; `demo`
is the example you just added. Drivers are discovered by executable
name — `tamias-driver-demo` — not by registration.

## 3. List and render views

```sh
pavo views
```

```
demo:board      /demo/board     Board
config:show     /config        Config
demo:deps       /demo/deps     Dependencies
…
```

```sh
pavo view demo:board
```

The default `text` format summarizes the ViewNode tree plus the data
bound to it. Try the other formats:

```sh
pavo view demo:board --format json       # raw ViewResult
pavo view demo:deps --format dot         # graph → graphviz
pavo view demo:deps --format mermaid     # graph → mermaid
```

## 4. Pass params

Views declare query bindings; callers pass params that merge into
them:

```sh
pavo view demo:board --param status=open
pavo view demo:board --param status=done
```

`--param k=v` accepts repeated pairs; values parse as JSON when
possible (`n=42`, `ok=true`).

## 5. See the merged chrome

```sh
pavo chrome
```

Lists every driver's contribution slots — navbar entries, dashboard
panels, statusbar items, routes — merged deterministically. The same
chrome drives the TUI rail and the web dashboard.

## What just happened

`pavo view demo:board` resolved the deep link `demo:board`, spawned
`tamias-driver-demo serve`, and spoke the wire:

```
→ {"op":"view","view":"board","params":{}}
← {"ok":true,"result":{"view":{…ViewSpec…},"data":{…}}}
```

The driver returned a declarative tree (`panel` → `kv` + `table` +
`markdown`) plus query-fed data; pavo's built-in renderers
interpreted it. No product code ran inside pavo — the driver is a
separate process, and the IR is the only thing that crossed the
boundary.

## Next

* [Deep links](/tutorials/deep-links) — stable URLs for views and params
* [Write a driver](/how-to/write-a-driver) — build your own
* [The wire protocol](/reference/wire-ops) — the ops in detail

url: /pavo/tutorials/deep-links.md

# Deep links

Every view has a stable `<driver>:<view>` ref. On the CLI it is an
argument; on the web it is a URL — the same link agents and humans
can drop into PRs, issues, and handoffs.

## The ref

```
pavo view demo:board
demo:board  →  route /demo/board  →  ViewSpec { id: "board" }
```

`pavo views` lists every ref; `pavo view --help` covers the CLI
flags (`--param`, `--format`, `--json`).

## Params in URLs

Views take params (`--param k=v` on the CLI). In URLs they can be
carried three ways — all normalize to the same `param.<k>=<v>`
pairs the bridge API understands:

```
/view/myco:item/id=T-001/verbose        path segments: one k=v each
/view/myco:item?id=T-001&verbose        bare query keys (no prefix)
/view/myco:item?param.id=T-001          legacy param.* form (still works)
```

Grammar details (parsed by `web/app/utils/view-link.ts`; the
no-build `/view/` stub in `pavo serve` speaks the same rules):

* The **first** path segment after `/view/` is the `<driver>:<view>`
  ref (the colon may be percent-encoded). Every later segment is one
  param: `key=value`, split at the **first** `=` (values may contain
  `=`); a bare `key` means an empty-string value; empty keys are
  dropped. So `/view/myco:item/T-001` sets param `T-001` to `""` —
  write `/view/myco:item/id=T-001` for a real param.
* Query keys are params too: bare `?k=v`, plus the legacy
  `?param.k=v` (prefix stripped).
* Precedence, lowest → highest: **path segments < bare query keys <
  `param.*` keys** — the bridge merges last-wins, so later sources
  override earlier ones on a key collision.
* Values parse as JSON when possible (`n=42`, `ok=true`, `j={…}`),
  else strings — identical to `--param` / `/api/view?param.*`.

## Serving the links

`pavo serve` prints `listening http://127.0.0.1:<port>`; open the
printed URL for the dashboard, or append a deep link directly:

```
http://127.0.0.1:7420/view/demo%3Aboard
http://127.0.0.1:7420/view/demo:board/status=open
```

With `cd web && npm run build` the bridge serves the Nuxt app;
without a build it serves a built-in landing page that still
understands `/view/` links.

## CLI equivalents

```sh
pavo view demo:board --param status=open
pavo open demo:deps          # TUI deep link (falls back to text off-TTY)
curl 'localhost:7420/api/view?ref=demo:board&param.status=open'
```

The `param.*` query convention is what the `/api/view` endpoint
already speaks — URL path segments and bare query keys are
normalized into it before the bridge sees them.

url: /pavo/how-to/install-a-driver.md
---
# Install a driver

Pavo discovers view providers as executables named
`tamias-driver-<type>` — the same convention tamias uses for content
drivers. There is no registry lookup and no config file: if the
binary is findable and answers `manifest`, pavo uses it.

## Discovery locations

1. **`PATH`** — any directory on your shell's `PATH`.
2. **`<tamias-home>/drivers/`** — `$TAMIAS_HOME` if set, else
   `$XDG_DATA_HOME/tamias`, else `~/.local/share/tamias`, else
   `./.tamias`. Symlinks work.

```bash
# on PATH (development)
export PATH="$PWD/examples/drivers/demo:$PATH"

# or into the tamias drivers dir (installed)
mkdir -p "${TAMIAS_HOME:-~/.local/share/tamias}/drivers"
ln -s "$PWD/examples/drivers/demo/tamias-driver-demo" \
      "${TAMIAS_HOME:-~/.local/share/tamias}/drivers/tamias-driver-demo"
```

## What counts as a pavo driver

A `tamias-driver-*` executable is a pavo driver when its `manifest`
answers a [`DriverManifest`](/reference/driver-manifest) with
`"serve"` in `verbs` (or `"pavo"` in `capabilities`). Drivers that
only do tamias install verbs are ignored by pavo.

```bash
printf '{"op":"manifest"}\n' | tamias-driver-demo serve
pavo drivers    # confirm discovery
```

## Installing real product drivers

Product drivers ship from their own repos — `tamias-driver-kuda`
(kuda), `tamias-driver-myco` (myco), `tamias-driver-cuora` (cuora),
`tamias-driver-sturn` (sturn), `tamias-driver-tamias` (tamias),
`tamias-driver-mimus` (mimus), `tamias-driver-sepia` (sepia),
`tamias-driver-bupha` (bupha). Install them like any tamias package
(they are `tamias-driver-*` content) or drop the binary on `PATH`:

```bash
tamias install git:9aia/myco//drivers/myco#v0.4.0   # example ref shape
# or:
cargo install --git https://github.com/9aia/myco tamias-driver-myco
```

Once installed they are discovered exactly like the examples —
`pavo drivers` lists them, `pavo views` lists their views.

Compiled drivers can also ride inside tamias packages: stage
prebuilt binaries under `drivers/bin/<rustc-target-triple>/`
(e.g. `drivers/bin/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tamias-driver-foo`) —
`tamias install --allow-drivers` picks the host triple, verifies the
payload digest, and lands an executable in `<tamias-home>/drivers/`.
See tamias's `examples/README.md` for the publish recipe.

## Verifying

```bash
./scripts/smoke-examples.sh   # repo root — runs the example set end-to-end
pavo-testkit                  # conformance: every driver passes the same suite
```

`pavo-testkit`'s `check_driver` runs the wire contract over any
driver binary; `FixtureDriver` builds fake drivers for host tests.
See [Write a driver](/how-to/write-a-driver).

---
url: /pavo/how-to/write-a-driver.md
---
# Write a driver

A pavo driver is an executable named `tamias-driver-<type>` that
answers the ndjson JSON-RPC wire on its `serve` verb — the same
convention as `myco serve`, `cuora serve`, `sepia serve`. The
driver owns its manifest and ViewNode trees; product state is only
needed when a `view`/`query` op actually runs.

## The contract in one paragraph

Spawned as `tamias-driver-<type> serve`, the driver reads one JSON
request per line on stdin and writes one JSON response per line on
stdout: `{"op":"manifest"}` → the
[`DriverManifest`](/reference/driver-manifest), `{"op":"views"}` →
view summaries, `{"op":"view","view":"…","params":{…}}` → a
`ViewResult` (tree + bound data), `{"op":"query",…}` → one query's
data. `{"op":"submit","view":"…","form":"…"?,"values":{…}}` →
a `SubmitResult` backs interactive `form` nodes (see
[Wire ops → submit](/reference/wire-ops#submit)). Every response is
`{"ok":true,"result":…}` or `{"ok":false,"error":"…"}`. Full spec:
[Wire ops](/reference/wire-ops).

## Minimal shape

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# tamias-driver-hello — stdlib only, like examples/drivers/*
import json, sys

def respond(req):
    op = req.get("op")
    if op == "manifest":
        return {"name": "hello", "title": "Hello", "version": "0.1.0",
                "verbs": ["manifest", "serve"], "capabilities": ["pavo"],
                "views": [view_spec()]}
    if op == "views":
        return [{"id": "hi", "title": "Hello", "route": "/hello/hi",
                 "queries": []}]
    if op == "view" and req.get("view") == "hi":
        return {"view": view_spec(), "data": {}}
    return {"ok": False}  # handled below

def view_spec():
    return {"id": "hi", "title": "Hello", "route": "/hello/hi",
            "queries": [],
            "root": {"kind": "markdown",
                     "text": "Hello from **pavo**!"}}

for line in sys.stdin:
    try:
        req = json.loads(line)
        if req.get("op") == "manifest":
            out = {"ok": True, "result": respond(req)}
        elif req.get("op") == "views":
            out = {"ok": True, "result": respond(req)}
        elif req.get("op") == "view":
            out = {"ok": True, "result": respond(req)}
        else:
            out = {"ok": False, "error": f"unknown op {req.get('op')!r}"}
    except Exception as e:
        out = {"ok": False, "error": str(e)}
    sys.stdout.write(json.dumps(out) + "\n")
    sys.stdout.flush()
```

Save it as `tamias-driver-hello`, `chmod +x`, put it on `PATH`, and
`pavo view hello:hi` renders the markdown node.

## Adding data: query bindings

Nodes pull data through `NodeBase.query` — a name that references a
[`QueryBinding`](/reference/driver-manifest) on the enclosing
`ViewSpec`:

```json
"queries": [{"name": "items", "op": "query", "params": {"kind": "items"}}],
"root": {"kind": "table",
         "query": "items",
         "columns": [{"key": "id", "title": "ID"},
                     {"key": "title", "title": "Title"}]}
```

When pavo resolves the view it calls the binding's `op` on your
`serve` and puts the result in `ViewResult.data["items"]`. The
`table` node reads `rows` from it (objects keyed by column `key`,
or inline `rows` arrays). A binding that fails lands as
`{"error": "…"}` in `data` — the view still renders (partial
degradation is the contract).

## Adding chrome: contributes

```json
"contributes": {
  "navbar":    [{"id": "hello:home", "title": "Hello", "route": "/hello/hi"}],
  "dashboard": [{"id": "hello:panel", "title": "Hello", "route": "/hello/hi"}],
  "statusbar": [{"id": "hello:status", "title": "ok", "route": "/hello/hi"}],
  "routes":    [{"id": "hello:admin", "title": "Admin", "route": "/hello/admin"}]
}
```

Slots merge across drivers by `priority` (lower wins, default
100\). Unknown slot names round-trip via `contributes.extra` — safe
to emit slots a given host doesn't know yet.

## Rust drivers

A driver can be any language — the wire is ndjson JSON. For Rust,
depend on the published contract crate instead of hand-rolling types:

```toml
pavo-protocol = "0.1"   # crates.io — manifests, ViewNode IR, ops
```

`pavo-testkit` (conformance suite) is not yet published — depend on it
by git (`github.com:9aia/pavo`) like the product drivers do. See
`crates/pavo-driver-config/` for a first-party example.

## The proxy pattern (recommended for real products)

Don't reimplement your product's data layer — translate the wire.
`examples/drivers/myco/` shows the canonical shape:

* `manifest`, `views`, and capability probes are answered **locally**
  — pavo discovers the driver even when the product isn't running.
* `view`/`query` ops resolve each binding through one persistent
  `myco serve` child speaking **JSON-RPC 2.0** (myco's wire is not
  pavo's `{"op":…}` envelope — translation is the driver's job).
* If the product is absent, return `ok:false` with a clear error;
  the host degrades that binding, not the whole chrome.

The production versions live in each product repo
(`tamias-driver-kuda`, `tamias-driver-myco`, `tamias-driver-cuora`).

## Stay compatible

* **Additive-only**: new optional fields and new `kind` variants may
  appear; never change existing spellings. Renderers ignore unknown
  kinds (they degrade to KV) — but don't rely on that for your own
  core UX.
* **`node`/`props` are open**: put renderer hints in `props`; hosts
  pass them through untouched.
* **Test against the contract**: `pavo-testkit`'s `check_driver`
  runs the conformance suite over your binary; `FixtureDriver` can
  stand in for your driver in host tests. Golden-fixture guidance:
  `cargo xtask test` runs the example drivers through the suite.

## Reference implementations

| Driver | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| `examples/drivers/demo/` | board (table+kv+markdown), deps `graph`, timeline `tree`; all chrome slots |
| `examples/drivers/myco/` | thin proxy onto `myco serve`'s JSON-RPC wire; degrades when myco is absent |
| `crates/pavo-driver-config/` | first-party Rust driver — the common config API (see [Use the config API](/how-to/use-config-api)) |

url: /pavo/how-to/write-a-renderer-plugin.md
---
# Write a renderer plugin

View-kind renderers are themselves tamias drivers — there is no
separate plugin ecosystem. A driver whose manifest carries
`renderers[]` claims ViewNode kinds on one or more surfaces and
answers the `render` wire op with a canonical
[`RenderModel`](/reference/wire-ops#rendermodel).

Use this when a built-in interpretation isn't good enough —
`examples/drivers/viz-graph/` claims `graph` and renders SVG,
ascii edge lists, and mermaid-free layouts the built-ins don't.

## 1. Declare the claim in the manifest

```json
"renderers": [{
  "id": "graph",
  "kinds": ["graph"],
  "priority": 50,
  "entry": "graph",
  "surfaces": {
    "cli": { "formats": ["svg", "ascii"] },
    "tui": true,
    "web": { "component": "viz-graph", "island": true }
  }
}]
```

* `kinds` — ViewNode `kind` strings, or `["*"]` for a catch-all.
  Explicit kinds beat `"*"`; lower `priority` wins conflicts
  (default 100); ties break by driver name then renderer id — the
  same policy chrome contributions use.
* `surfaces.cli.formats` — the `--format` values you claim;
  **empty = wildcard** (you handle every format asked, including
  `text`). Built-in names are claimable: listing `dot`, `mermaid`,
  or `text` overrides the built-in renderer *for your claimed
  nodes* — unclaimed nodes keep the built-in output. `json` is
  never claimable (the raw `ViewResult` dump is host-owned).
* `surfaces.tui` — `true` to render on the ratatui host.
* `surfaces.web` — `component` is a hint for rich mounts;
  `island: true` marks output needing client-side execution.

A driver may declare renderers **with zero views** — a pure plugin
ships no routes of its own.

## 2. Answer the `render` op

For every node whose kind is claimed on the asking surface, the
host sends:

```
{"op":"render","kind":"graph","node":{…ViewNode verbatim…},
 "data":{…view data map…},"surface":"cli|tui|web","format":"…"?}
```

* `node` is the raw ViewNode JSON — unknown/future fields reach you
  untouched.
* `data` is the view's query-binding map verbatim — resolve
  `node.query` against it yourself.
* `surface` is `"cli"`, `"tui"`, or `"web"` (open string — hosts may
  add surfaces).
* `format` is the surface's format hint (`"svg"`, `"ascii"`, …)
  when one applies.

Respond with a `RenderModel` (`{"ok":true,"result":{…}}`):

| variant       | shape                                        | CLI            | TUI          | web              |
|---------------|----------------------------------------------|----------------|--------------|------------------|
| `rows`        | `{type,headers,aligns?,rows}`                | aligned table  | table rows   | `<table>`        |
| `svg`         | `{type,markup}` — self-contained `<svg>`     | raw markup     | `[svg]` hint | `v-html` island  |
| `text`        | `{type,lines}`                               | lines          | lines        | `<pre>`          |
| `placeholder` | `{type,component,props?}`                    | `[component]`  | box + detail | named component  |

Rules:

* **Built-ins are not reserved** — claim `graph` (or any kind) and
  you override built-in rendering on the surfaces you declare.
* **Fallback is mandatory** — when no plugin claims a kind+surface,
  or `render` errors/times out, hosts use the built-in
  interpretation. Plugin failure must never break a view.
* **No HTML in RenderModel** — self-contained markup is `svg` only.
* Unknown `type` values degrade like `placeholder` on every
  surface — keep to the four variants.

## 3. Test it

```bash
export PATH="$PWD/examples/drivers/viz-graph:$PATH"
pavo drivers                          # viz-graph … renderers:1
pavo view demo:deps --format svg      # plugin SVG (claims svg+ascii)
pavo view demo:deps --format mermaid  # built-in — plugin doesn't claim it
pavo view demo:deps --format ascii    # plugin edge list
```

`/api/renderers` on `pavo serve` lists every claim;
`/api/render` proxies a `render` op for the web surface's plugin
path. `pavo-testkit` conformance covers drivers that answer
`render` — see `check_driver`.

## Reference

`examples/drivers/viz-graph/tamias-driver-viz-graph` is the whole
implementation (~200 lines of Python): manifest claim, `render`
dispatch on `kind`/`surface`/`format`, three RenderModel shapes.
Copy it.

url: /pavo/how-to/serve-web.md
---
# Serve the web surface

`pavo serve` is the localhost HTTP bridge between the browser and
the driver plane — the only transport the web host uses. It binds
`127.0.0.1` (localhost dev tool; CORS `*` on `/api/*`), prints
`listening http://127.0.0.1:<port>` as its first stdout line, and
serves two things:

* **`/api/*`** — JSON `{"ok":…,"result"/"error"}` envelopes over the
  same `Host` the CLI uses:
  `GET /api/health|drivers|views|chrome|view|raw|query|submit|renderers|render`
* **`/*`** — static files from `web/.output/public`, then `web/dist`,
  then `$PAVO_WEB_DIR`; with no build present it serves a built-in
  landing page that still understands `/view/` deep links.

## Dev workflow (two terminals)

```bash
# 1. the bridge (7420 matches the Nuxt dev proxy default)
export PATH="$PWD/examples/drivers/demo:$PATH"
pavo serve --port 7420        # or: cargo run -p pavo -- serve --port 7420

# 2. the app
cd web && npm install && npm run dev    # http://localhost:3000
```

`web/server/api/[...].ts` proxies `/api/*` to the bridge in dev —
target precedence: `PAVO_API_TARGET` > `NUXT_PUBLIC_PAVO_API` >
`http://127.0.0.1:7420`.

## Production-ish flow

```bash
cd web && npm run build      # static prerender → .output/public
pavo serve                   # auto-detects web/.output/public
```

Open the printed `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/` — the dashboard lists
drivers, views (deep links `/view/demo%3Aboard`), and chrome
contributions; `/api/*` is same-origin, no CORS needed.

`npm run generate` is equivalent (`nuxt generate`).
`NITRO_PRESET=node-server npm run build` produces a standalone SSR
build instead — then `server/api/*` also works and
`NUXT_PUBLIC_PAVO_API` points the browser at the bridge directly.

## Environment variables

| Var | Where | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NUXT_PUBLIC_PAVO_API` | build/dev | absolute bridge base, e.g. `http://127.0.0.1:7420`. Empty (default) = same-origin `/api/…`. |
| `PAVO_API_TARGET` | `nuxt dev` only | proxy target for `server/api/[...].ts`. |
| `NITRO_PRESET` | build | `static` (default) or `node-server`. |
| `PAVO_WEB_DIR` | `pavo serve` | explicit web-root override for static files. |
| `PAVO_CONFIG` | `tamias-driver-config` | explicit config file path (see [Use the config API](/how-to/use-config-api)). |

`pavo serve --port 0` picks a free port and prints it.

## What the web app renders

`web/app/components/ViewNode.vue` interprets the ViewNode IR
recursively — panel/row/column layouts, table, tree, kv, markdown,
interactive form (`submit_op` → `FormView` island hitting `/api/submit`), embed placeholder, KV degradation for unknown
kinds. `graph` nodes render in `GraphIsland.vue`, a client-only
SVG island (deterministic circle/spiral layout) — the *fallback*:
a renderer plugin claiming `graph` for the `web` surface renders
its canonical `RenderModel` via `/api/render` instead (placeholder
while in flight, built-in only if the plugin fails or doesn't
claim the kind). Driver-contributed `routes` link
out; only views render natively in v1.

## Security notes

`npm audit` currently reports transitive vulnerabilities inside the
Nuxt/Nitro build chain (see `web/README.md` for the breakdown);
exposure is limited to the local dev/build toolchain — the shipped
artifact is static files served by `pavo serve`. Re-check on Nuxt
upgrades.

---

---
url: /pavo/how-to/use-config-api.md
---
# Use the config API

`tamias-driver-config` is the suite's **common config API** — a
first-party pavo driver (Rust, in the workspace) that answers
namespaced config queries over the `serve` wire. It is a
convention layered on the `query` op, not part of the v1 wire
contract itself: drivers that need product or host config spawn it
and issue queries — they never open config files themselves.

```bash
printf '%s\n' '{"op":"query","query":"get","params":{"key":"myco.theme"}}' \
  | tamias-driver-config serve
# → {"ok":true,"result":{"query":"get","data":{"key":"myco.theme","value":"dark","found":true}}}
```

Products may later adopt the API natively; until then this driver
is the one config surface. It installs with pavo
(`cargo xtask install`) and contributes a `config:show` view plus a
statusbar entry.

## Queries

| query      | params             | data                                          |
| ---------- | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| `get`      | `key` (dotted)     | `{key, value, found}`                         |
| `set`      | `key`, `value`     | `{key, value, path, written}` or `{error}`    |
| `resolve`  | —                  | merged config tree (nested JSON object)       |
| `config`   | —                  | merged config flattened to dotted keys        |
| `sources`  | —                  | every contributing layer, in precedence order |

`set` writes the **project-level** file: the `--config`/`PAVO_CONFIG`
path when one was given, else the nearest `pavo.toml`/`pavo.json`
found walking up from the cwd, else a fresh `./pavo.toml`. Dotted
keys are supported (`server.port` creates the `[server]` table);
TOML writes preserve comments/formatting (`toml_edit`), JSON is
rewritten pretty-printed. `null` and nested objects can't be stored
in TOML — use dotted keys for tables.

## Resolution order

Layers merge low → high precedence (later wins per-key, nested
tables merge recursively):

1. **defaults** — `theme=dark`, `statusbar=true`, `refresh_ms=5000`
2. **global** — `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pavo/pavo.{toml,json}` or
   `~/.config/pavo/pavo.{toml,json}`
3. **project** — `pavo.toml` and `pavo.json` in every ancestor of the
   cwd, filesystem root → cwd (nearest file wins)
4. **explicit** — `--config <path>` on argv (manual `serve` only —
   pavo's spawned `serve` can't pass argv) or `$PAVO_CONFIG`
5. **env** — `PAVO_CONFIG_*` scalar overrides:
   `PAVO_CONFIG_THEME=light` → `theme`;
   `PAVO_CONFIG_MYCO__THEME=x` → `myco.theme` (`__` = dot, `_` =
   literal underscore). Values parse as JSON when possible.

Formats: **TOML** and **JSON**. **YAML is unsupported** — no yaml dep
in the workspace tree; `.yaml`/`.yml` files surface as `error` rows in
`sources` rather than being silently misparsed.

## Views

| Deep link          | Route              | Shows                                        |
| ------------------ | ------------------ | -------------------------------------------- |
| `config:show`      | `/config`          | resolved KV + sources table + resolution doc |
| `config:sources`   | `/config/sources`  | provenance table only                        |

Contributes a `statusbar` entry linking to `/config`.

```bash
pavo view config:show
pavo view config:sources
PAVO_CONFIG_THEME=light pavo view config:show   # env override wins
```

## Keys are namespaced

Callers use dotted paths — `myco.theme`, `kuda.index`, `pavo.refresh_ms`
— never file paths or raw TOML. `resolve` returns the merged tree;
`sources` returns every contributing layer so UIs can show
provenance ("this value came from `~/.config/pavo/pavo.toml`").

---

---
url: /pavo/reference/cli.md
---
# CLI reference

```
Visualization host for the 9aia tool suite

Usage: pavo [COMMAND]

Commands:
  drivers     List discovered tamias-driver-* executables that speak pavo
  views       List every <driver>:<view> ref with title/route
  chrome      Show the merged contribution slots
  view        Resolve a deep link and render it
  query       Raw query-op passthrough to a driver
  submit      Submit a form's field values (submit wire op)
  serve       Run the localhost HTTP bridge for the web host
  open        Hand off to pavo-tui (falls back to `view` text off-TTY)
  manifest    Print the machine-readable capability manifest
  schema      Print the verb schema
  help        Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help     Print help
  -V, --version  Print version
```

`--json` is a per-subcommand flag on the listing/query verbs;
`view --format json` is its machine-readable mode. Errors go to
stderr; exit codes are CI-meaningful: `0` ok, `1` view/driver error,
`2` usage.

## drivers

```sh
pavo drivers [--json]
```

Lists every discovered `tamias-driver-*` that speaks pavo — name,
title, version, view count, renderer count, contributes summary.
Discovery scans `PATH` and `<tamias-home>/drivers/`
(`$TAMIAS_HOME` → `$XDG_DATA_HOME/tamias` → `~/.local/share/tamias`
→ `./.tamias`).

## views

```sh
pavo views [--driver <name>] [--json]
```

Every view as a `<driver>:<view>` ref with title, route, and query
names. `--driver` filters to one driver.

## chrome

```sh
pavo chrome [--json]
```

The merged contribution slots — `navbar`, `dashboard`, `statusbar`,
`routes`, plus forward-compat `extra` slots — resolved across all
drivers by priority.

## view

```sh
pavo view <driver>:<view> [--param k=v …] [--format FMT] [--json]
```

Resolves the deep link and renders the ViewNode tree plus bound
data.

| `--format` | Output |
| --- | --- |
| `text` (default) | summary of the tree + bound data |
| `json` | raw `ViewResult` |
| `dot` | graph nodes → graphviz |
| `mermaid` | graph nodes → mermaid |
| `<plugin>` | any format a renderer plugin claims (e.g. `svg`, `ascii`) |

Renderer plugins take precedence per node: a plugin listing a
built-in format name (`text`/`dot`/`mermaid`) in
`renderers[].surfaces.cli.formats` overrides it for the kinds it
claims; unclaimed nodes keep the built-in output. `json` is
host-owned and never routed to plugins.

`--param k=v` merges caller params into every query binding;
repeatable, values parse as JSON when possible. `--json` prints the
machine-readable envelope.

## query

```sh
pavo query <driver> <query> [--param k=v …] [--json]
```

Raw `query` op passthrough — `{"op":"query","query":"<query>",
"params":{…}}` — for probing a driver's data without a view.

## submit

```sh
pavo submit <driver>:<view> [--form <id>] [--param k=v …] [--json]
```

Sends the `submit` wire op — the form-interaction verb — with the
given field values (`--param key=value`, repeatable; values parse as
JSON when possible). `--form` picks a specific form node when the
view carries several. Prints the driver's `SubmitResult` message and
data; per-field validation `errors` exit 1 so CI can gate on them.
`--json` dumps the full `SubmitResult` (including any updated
`view`). Example: `pavo submit config:edit --param key=myco.theme --param value=dark`.

## serve

```sh
pavo serve [--port N]
```

The localhost HTTP bridge (`127.0.0.1`; `--port 0` picks a free
port). First stdout line is `listening http://127.0.0.1:<port>`.
Endpoints and static serving: [Serve the web surface](/how-to/serve-web).

## open

```sh
pavo open [<driver>:<view>]
```

Hands off to `pavo-tui` with the deep link, or the bare dashboard
when no target is given. On a non-TTY it falls back to `pavo view`
text output.

## manifest / schema

```sh
pavo manifest   # the CLI's own capability manifest (sibling convention)
pavo schema     # the verb schema
```

---

---
url: /pavo/reference/view-nodes.md
---
# ViewNode IR

The declarative UI tree a driver emits and every pavo renderer
(CLI, TUI, web) interprets. Wire shape: each node is a JSON object
with a `"kind"` discriminator — internally tagged, no wrapper
envelope. Rust source of truth:
`crates/pavo-protocol/src/view_node.rs`;
`protocol/v1/view-node.schema.json` mirrors it.

```json
{ "kind": "table", "title": "Board", "query": "items",
  "columns": [{ "key": "id", "title": "ID" }],
  "rows": [["T-001", "pavo scaffold"]] }
```

## Shared fields (NodeBase)

Every kind flattens these to the top level:

| field | type | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | string? | stable id — deep-link target, diffing, expansion state |
| `title` | string? | heading the renderer may show above the node |
| `query` | string? | names a `QueryBinding` on the enclosing `ViewSpec`; kind-specific meaning (`table`→`rows`, `kv`→`pairs`, `tree`→`items`, `graph`→`nodes`/`edges`) |
| `description` | string? | longer help text (tooltips, help panes) |
| `props` | object | renderer hints (`density`, `direction`, `collapsed`, …); renderers ignore unknown keys |

## Kinds

| `kind` | purpose | key fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `panel` | titled container grouping children | `children[]` |
| `row` | horizontal layout | `children[]`, `gap?` |
| `column` | vertical layout | `children[]`, `gap?` |
| `table` | tabular data | `columns[]` (`key`,`title`,`align?`,`width?`), `rows?` (inline cell arrays win over query data), `sortable?` |
| `tree` | hierarchical items | `items[]` (`id?`,`label`,`detail?`,`icon?`,`children[]`,`props`), `expandable?` |
| `graph` | nodes + edges; layout is the renderer's problem | `nodes[]` (`id`,`label`,`kind?`,`props`), `edges[]` (`from`,`to`,`label?`), `layout?` (`"dot"`,`"mermaid"`,`"layered"`,…) |
| `form` | input fields + submit op — **interactive** via the `submit` wire op | `fields[]`, `submit_op?`, `submit_label?` |
| `kv` | key/value pairs — detail panes, metadata, **universal degradation target** | `pairs[]` (`key`,`value`,`kind?`) |
| `markdown` | free-form markdown | `text` |
| `embed` | escape hatch for rich renderers | `component` (registry/web-component name); component props ride in `props` |

### Field details

* **`table.columns[].key`** — for query-fed data, rows arrive as
  objects keyed by `key`; inline `rows` are positional arrays of
  arbitrary JSON cells (renderers stringify).
* **`table.rows`** — inline rows ship static previews; when both
  inline rows and `query` data exist, inline wins.
* **`tree.items`** — recursive; `id` is required for interactive
  trees, optional for static previews. Omitted `items` (vs `[]`)
  matters on the typed round-trip so an empty inline list can't
  shadow query-bound data.
* **`graph`** — the IR floor covers structure only. Real layout is
  an `embed`/renderer-plugin concern; `layout` is a hint renderers
  may ignore.
* **`form.fields[].kind`** — `text` (default), `textarea`, `number`,
  `bool`, `select` (with `options`). `required`, `default`, `value`,
  `hint`, `editable` (default `true`; `false` renders read-only and
  is never submitted), and `placeholder` are supported. Submission
  goes through the [`submit` op](/reference/wire-ops#submit); the
  form node's `id` is the `form` param when a view has several
  forms, and `submit_op` names the driver-side action (`"set"`,
  `"update"`, `"add"`, …).
* **`embed`** — for visuals no built-in model covers (live graphs,
  timelines, WASM). `component` resolves against the host's
  renderer registry and, on web, registered components.

## Degradation is mandatory

Renderers that meet an unknown `kind` must degrade to generic
key/value rendering rather than failing — forward compatibility is
a host obligation, and the protocol is additive-only within v1. The
same applies to `props` keys and enum values.

---

---
url: /pavo/reference/wire-ops.md
---
# Wire ops

The ndjson JSON-RPC convention every pavo driver speaks on its
`serve` verb — the same framing as `tamias-serve`, `myco serve`,
`cuora serve`, `sepia serve`. One JSON object per line on stdin,
one response per line on stdout.

Rust source of truth: `crates/pavo-protocol/src/wire.rs`;
`protocol/v1/wire.schema.json` mirrors it.

## Envelope

Requests are discriminated by `op` (internally tagged, lowercase):

```json
{"op":"manifest"}
{"op":"views"}
{"op":"view","view":"board","params":{"status":"open"}}
{"op":"query","query":"items","params":{"limit":5}}
{"op":"render","kind":"graph","node":{…},"data":{…},
 "surface":"cli","format":"svg"}
{"op":"submit","view":"edit","form":"set-config",
 "values":{"key":"myco.theme","value":"dark"}}
```

Responses:

```json
{"ok":true,"result":…}
{"ok":false,"error":"…"}
```

Fields for the non-matching arm are absent (not null) — consumers
match on `ok` alone. A driver must never crash the wire: malformed
input and serialization failures become `ok:false` responses.

## Ops

### `manifest`

`{"op":"manifest"}` → [`DriverManifest`](/reference/driver-manifest).
Discovery verb — cheap, must not require product state. This is how
pavo decides a `tamias-driver-*` is a view driver (`"serve"` in
`verbs` or `"pavo"` in `capabilities`).

### `views`

`{"op":"views"}` → `Vec<ViewSummary>` — `{id, title, route,
description?, queries[]}` per view, without the `root` trees.
Lightweight listing for `pavo views` and picker UIs; full trees come
from `view`.

### `view`

`{"op":"view","view":"<id>","params":{…}}` →
[`ViewResult`](/reference/wire-ops#viewresult):

```json
{"view": { …ViewSpec including root tree… },
 "data": { "<binding-name>": <payload>, … }}
```

The host resolves each `QueryBinding` on the spec (calling its `op`
with static params merged under caller `params`) and puts results
in `data` keyed by binding name — `data["items"]` feeds every node
whose `query == "items"`. **Partial degradation**: a binding that
fails appears as `{"error": "…"}` in `data` rather than failing the
whole view.

### `query`

`{"op":"query","query":"<name>","params":{…}}` →
`{"query":"<name>","data":<payload>}` — execute a single named
query binding, or a raw product op for thin drivers. Powers
`pavo query` and ad-hoc data probes; also the transport the
[config API](/how-to/use-config-api) rides (`query` = `get`/`set`/
`resolve`/`sources`/`config`).

### `render`

`{"op":"render","kind":"<kind>","node":{…ViewNode verbatim…},
"data":{…view data map…},"surface":"cli|tui|web","format":"…"?}`
→ [`RenderModel`](/reference/wire-ops#rendermodel) — the
renderer-plugin verb. Only sent to drivers whose manifest claims
the node's kind on the asking surface (see
[Renderer plugins](/explanation/renderer-plugins)).

* `node` — raw ViewNode JSON, passed untyped so unknown/future
  fields survive.
* `data` — the same binding map `view` results carry.
* `surface` — open string; hosts may add surfaces.
* `format` — the surface's format hint when one applies.

### `submit`

`{"op":"submit","view":"<id>","form":"<id>"?,"values":{…}}` →
[`SubmitResult`](#submitresult) — the form-submission verb. A
surface collects the editable fields of a `form` ViewNode and posts
their `key` → value pairs here.

* `view` — the view the form lives in (same namespace as `view`).
* `form` — optional form-node `id` when the view carries several
  forms; absent = the driver's default/first form.
* `values` — submitted field values keyed by `FormField.key`.

The driver resolves the form node, reads its `submit_op`
(driver-defined: `"set"`, `"update"`, `"add"`, …), and answers a
`SubmitResult`. Drivers without form support answer `ok:false`.
`pavo submit <driver>:<view> --param k=v …` is the CLI face;
`GET /api/submit?ref=…&values={…}` the web-bridge face.

## Types

### ViewSummary

`{id, title, route, description?, queries[]}` — a `ViewSpec` minus
`root`, for cheap listing.

### ViewResult

`{view: ViewSpec, data: {<binding>: payload}}` — the resolved view.
Failed bindings carry `{"error": "…"}` payloads.

### QueryResult

`{query: string, data: any}` — one binding's data payload; shape is
driver-defined, hosts pass it through verbatim.

### SubmitResult

`{message?, errors?, data?, view?}` — every field optional; a bare
`{"message":"…"}` is complete. `errors` is a per-field validation
map keyed by `FormField.key` — non-empty means the driver *rejected*
the submit (hosts re-render with the messages; `pavo submit` exits
1\). `view`, when present, is a fresh `ViewResult` to swap in.
Unknown fields survive typed round-trips.

### RenderModel

The canonical intermediate output a renderer plugin emits —
internally tagged on `"type"`:

| `type` | shape | CLI | TUI | web |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `rows` | `{type, headers[], aligns?[], rows[][]}` | aligned table | table rows | `<table>` |
| `svg` | `{type, markup}` — self-contained `<svg>` | raw markup | `[svg]` hint | `v-html` island |
| `text` | `{type, lines[]}` | lines | lines | `<pre>` |
| `placeholder` | `{type, component, props?}` | `[component]` | box + detail | named component |

Rules: no HTML in RenderModel (self-contained markup is `svg`
only); unknown `type` degrades like `placeholder`; plugins needing
richer output use `placeholder` or `svg`.

## Versioning

**Additive-only within v1**: new optional fields, new `op`s, new
`kind`/`type` variants may appear at any time; existing fields and
spellings never change meaning. Unknown ops are protocol errors —
hosts surface the driver's raw error text. Breaking changes bump the
version directory (`protocol/v2/`) with a migration note; v1 stays
frozen for existing drivers.

---

---
url: /pavo/reference/driver-manifest.md
---
# Driver manifest

What `tamias-driver-<type> manifest` (or `{"op":"manifest"}` on the
`serve` wire) answers — the discovery contract. Pavo reads it
without spawning `serve`, so routes and chrome contributions are
listable even when the product isn't running.

Rust source of truth: `crates/pavo-protocol/src/manifest.rs`;
`protocol/v1/driver-manifest.schema.json` mirrors it.

```json
{
  "name": "myco",
  "title": "Myco",
  "icon": "🗂️",
  "version": "0.4.0",
  "verbs": ["manifest", "serve"],
  "capabilities": ["pavo"],
  "contributes": { "navbar": [...], "routes": [...] },
  "views": [ { "id": "board", "route": "/myco/board", "root": {…} } ],
  "renderers": [ { "id": "graph", "kinds": ["graph"], "surfaces": {…} } ]
}
```

## Fields

| field | type | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string | the `<type>` in `tamias-driver-<type>`; namespaces routes (`/<name>/<view>`) |
| `title` | string | human-facing title for chrome (navbar, window titles) |
| `icon` | string? | emoji, icon name, or renderer-resolvable path |
| `version` | string | semver |
| `verbs` | string\[] | wire verbs beyond tamias install verbs; pavo treats a driver as a view driver iff `"serve"` is listed (or `capabilities` contains `"pavo"`) |
| `capabilities` | string\[] | free-form role tags (`"pavo"`, `"config"`, `"chrome"`) |
| `contributes` | object | chrome slots — see below |
| `views` | ViewSpec\[] | views the driver renders |
| `renderers` | RendererDecl\[] | view-kind renderer plugins — may appear with zero views |

## contributes

Named places in pavo's chrome where drivers register entries. The
four built-in slots:

| slot | lands in |
| --- | --- |
| `navbar` | top navigation bar (web/TUI chrome) |
| `dashboard` | the shared dashboard route — composable panels from many drivers |
| `statusbar` | bottom status bar — one-line summaries |
| `routes` | standalone routes the driver owns outside its views |

Unknown slots are preserved via `contributes.extra` (serde
flatten) — newer drivers degrade gracefully on older hosts.

### Contribution

```json
{"id": "demo:board", "title": "Board", "route": "/demo/board",
 "priority": 100, "icon": "📋"}
```

`id` is namespaced `<driver>:<id>` by convention so contributions
never collide; `route` is host-relative; `priority` orders entries
within a slot (lower wins, default 100, ties by discovery order).

## views — ViewSpec

```json
{"id": "board", "title": "Board", "route": "/demo/board",
 "description": "…",
 "queries": [{"name": "items", "op": "query",
              "params": {"kind": "items"}}],
 "root": { "kind": "panel", "children": [ …ViewNode… ] }}
```

* `id` — unique within the driver; `<driver>:<id>` is the deep link.
* `route` — the host-relative path the view answers.
* `queries` — named data sources the tree references via
  `NodeBase.query`. Each `QueryBinding` has `name` (what nodes
  reference), `op` (the wire op the host calls — typically
  `"query"`), and static `params` merged under caller-supplied view
  params.
* `root` — the declarative [`ViewNode`](/reference/view-nodes) tree.

## renderers — RendererDecl

```json
{"id": "graph", "kinds": ["graph"], "priority": 50,
 "entry": "graph",
 "surfaces": {
   "cli":  {"formats": ["svg", "ascii"]},
   "tui":  true,
   "web":  {"component": "viz-graph", "island": true}}}
```

| field | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | renderer id — namespaced `<driver>:<id>` by convention |
| `kinds` | node kinds claimed — ViewNode `kind` strings or `"*"` catch-all; explicit beats `"*"`, lower `priority` wins, ties by driver name then renderer id |
| `surfaces` | per-surface support; absent surface = unsupported |
| `surfaces.cli.formats` | `--format` values claimed; **empty = wildcard** (all formats incl. `text`) |
| `surfaces.tui` | `true` renders plugin nodes on the ratatui host |
| `surfaces.web.component` / `.island` | component hint; `island: true` = needs client-side execution |
| `priority` | ordering hint, default 100 |
| `entry` | optional entry-point hint (reserved; hosts currently always use the wire) |

Claims are canonical per node on their declared surfaces — a plugin
listing a built-in `--format` name (`text`/`dot`/`mermaid`) overrides
it for claimed nodes (`json` stays host-owned); unclaimed
kinds/surfaces keep built-in rendering, and plugin failure degrades
to it. See [Write a renderer plugin](/how-to/write-a-renderer-plugin)
and [Renderer plugins](/explanation/renderer-plugins).

---

---
url: /pavo/reference/config.md
---
# Config

Host/product configuration for the pavo suite flows through the
**config API** — `tamias-driver-config`, a first-party driver that
answers namespaced `query` ops over the `serve` wire. There is no
`pavo.toml` read directly by the host; drivers and products query
the config driver (or adopt the API natively later).

Full contract: `crates/pavo-driver-config/README.md`; usage:
[Use the config API](/how-to/use-config-api).

## Queries

| query | params | returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `get` | `key` (dotted) | `{key, value, found}` |
| `set` | `key`, `value` | `{key, value, path, written}` |
| `resolve` | — | merged config tree (nested JSON) |
| `config` | — | merged config flattened to dotted keys |
| `sources` | — | every contributing layer, in precedence order |

Keys are namespaced dotted paths (`myco.theme`, `kuda.index`) —
callers never read config files directly.

## Layers (low → high precedence)

1. **defaults** — `theme=dark`, `statusbar=true`, `refresh_ms=5000`
2. **global** — `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pavo/pavo.{toml,json}` or
   `~/.config/pavo/pavo.{toml,json}`
3. **project** — `pavo.toml` and `pavo.json` in every ancestor of the
   cwd, filesystem root → cwd (nearest file wins)
4. **explicit** — `--config <path>` on argv (manual `serve` only) or
   `$PAVO_CONFIG`
5. **env** — `PAVO_CONFIG_*` scalar overrides

## Environment variables

| Var | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `TAMIAS_HOME` | tamias home override — also the default drivers dir parent (`$TAMIAS_HOME/drivers`) |
| `XDG_DATA_HOME` | fallback parent for `<tamias-home>` (`$XDG_DATA_HOME/tamias`) |
| `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | fallback parent for global config (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pavo/`) |
| `PAVO_CONFIG` | explicit config file path for `tamias-driver-config` |
| `PAVO_CONFIG_*` | env overrides — `PAVO_CONFIG_THEME=light` → `theme`; `PAVO_CONFIG_MYCO__THEME=x` → `myco.theme` (`__` = dot, `_` = literal underscore); values parse as JSON when possible |
| `PAVO_WEB_DIR` | `pavo serve` static web-root override |
| `NUXT_PUBLIC_PAVO_API` | web app: absolute bridge base (empty = same-origin `/api`) |
| `PAVO_API_TARGET` | `nuxt dev` only: `/api/*` proxy target |
| `NITRO_PRESET` | web build: `static` (default) or `node-server` |

## Formats

**TOML** and **JSON** only — no YAML dependency in the workspace
tree. `.yaml`/`.yml` files surface as `error` rows in `sources`
rather than being silently misparsed.

`set` writes the project-level file (explicit path → nearest
`pavo.toml`/`pavo.json` → fresh `./pavo.toml`); TOML writes preserve
comments via `toml_edit`. `null` and nested objects can't be stored
in TOML — use dotted keys for tables.

Rustdoc for every workspace crate — public APIs are
documented at source (doc comments).

* [pavo-testkit](/pavo/api/pavo_testkit/index.html) — adapter

* [pavo](/pavo/api/pavo/index.html) — binary

# Architecture

Pavo is the visualization **host** for the 9aia org's tool suite —
the factory's screen. Named for *Pavo* — the peafowl genus; the
display animal.

The core idea: **products ship drivers, not UIs.** A product
(kuda, myco, cuora, …) ships a `tamias-driver-<type>` executable
that speaks an ndjson JSON-RPC wire and emits a declarative
**ViewNode IR** — a tree of typed nodes (`panel`, `table`, `tree`,
`graph`, `form`, `kv`, `markdown`, `embed`, `row`, `column`) plus
view-model data. Pavo's renderers — CLI, TUI, web — interpret those
trees natively. There is no `<product> ui` per product; pavo is the
single entry point, and a driver installed once visualizes on every
surface.

```
tamias-driver-* (serve, stdio)          pavo host
┌──────────────────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ manifest → routes+chrome │ ───▶ │ pavo-core Host              │
│ view    → ViewNode + data│ ◀─── │  discovery → manifests      │
│ query   → data payload   │      │  → DriverClient (1 proc/    │
│ render  → RenderModel    │      │    driver, timeout+restart) │
└──────────────────────────┘      │  → merge chrome, resolve     │
                                  │    <driver>:<view> links     │
        renderers: CLI · TUI · web│  → view-model cache          │
                                  └─────────────────────────────┘
```

## The layers

* **`pavo-protocol`** — the public wire contract: driver manifests,
  ViewNode IR, RenderModel, ndjson ops. Pure serde, no I/O. The
  JSON Schemas in `protocol/v1/` are hand-maintained mirrors;
  versioning is additive-only within v1.
* **`pavo-core`** — host core: driver discovery (PATH +
  `<tamias-home>/drivers/`), contribution merge, per-driver
  `DriverClient`s, ViewNode walk/evaluate helpers, the renderer
  registry, the view-model TTL cache. Sync and std-only.
* **`pavo-cli`** (`pavo`) — the binary: `drivers`/`views`/`chrome`/
  `view`/`query`/`serve`/`open` verbs, `--json` everywhere, and the
  protocol conformance harness. Also `pavo serve`, the localhost
  HTTP bridge for the web host.
* **`pavo-tui`** (`pavo-tui`) — the ratatui surface: driver rail,
  ViewNode canvas, detail pane, contribution-driven chrome.
* **`pavo-testkit`** — conformance: `FixtureDriver` builds fake
  `tamias-driver-*` executables, `check_driver` runs the wire
  contract suite, record/replay transcripts give renderers
  deterministic sessions.
* **`pavo-driver-config`** (`tamias-driver-config`) — first-party
  driver: the common config API (namespaced `query` ops over
  layered TOML/JSON config).
* **`web/`** — the Nuxt 4 SSR shell + client-side data islands,
  served as static files by `pavo serve`.
* **`examples/drivers/`** — reference drivers: `demo` (full IR +
  chrome), `myco` (thin proxy pattern), `viz-graph` (renderer
  plugin).

| crate | layer | purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `pavo-protocol` | domain | Wire contract — driver manifests, ViewNode IR, ndjson ops (the public API) |
| `pavo-core` | host | Host core — tamias driver discovery, contribution merge, per-driver clients, view-model cache |
| `pavo-driver-config` | adapter | tamias-driver-config — the common config API driver for the 9aia suite (pavo view driver) |
| `pavo-testkit` | adapter | Recorded driver sessions → conformance fixtures for all pavo surfaces |
| `pavo-tui` | adapter | ratatui host — chrome slots + ViewNode renderer for pavo |
| `pavo` | binary | pavo — visualization host: discover tamias drivers, render their views (CLI/TUI/web) |

## The wire

Drivers are spawned per surface need: pavo keeps one `serve`
process per driver (`DriverClient`), speaks `{"op":…}` →
`{"ok":…}` ndjson, and caches view models briefly. Discovery is
cheap — `manifest` answers without product state, so `pavo drivers`
and `pavo views` work even when the underlying product isn't
running. Full contract: [Wire ops](/reference/wire-ops),
[Driver manifest](/reference/driver-manifest).

## Deep links are the UI

A view is a `<driver>:<view>` ref plus optional params. On the CLI
it's an argument; on the web it's a URL
(`/view/myco:item/id=T-001`) that agents and humans can drop into
PRs, issues, and handoffs. The TUI takes the same ref via
`pavo open`. See [Deep links](/tutorials/deep-links).

## Why this shape

See [Why declarative views](/explanation/why-declarative) and
[Boundaries](/explanation/boundaries).

---

---
url: /pavo/explanation/why-declarative.md
---
# Why declarative views

Pavo could have let every product ship its own TUI, its own web
app, its own CLI flags. Instead drivers emit a **declarative**
tree — data, not code — and hosts interpret it. The reasons:

## One driver, every surface

A `ViewNode` tree is surface-agnostic JSON. The same `myco:board`
spec renders as an aligned table on the CLI, ratatui widgets in the
TUI, and DOM in the web app — with zero per-surface driver code.
When a fifth surface appears (a chat bridge, an editor panel), it
interprets the same IR.

## Drivers stay dumb and safe

A driver is a separate process speaking a narrow wire. It can't
inject HTML, run host code, or touch renderer internals — the worst
a buggy driver can do is emit a malformed tree, which degrades to
KV. That boundary is what lets pavo host *untrusted-ish* product
drivers discovered on `PATH`.

## Degradation is a feature, not a fallback

The protocol is **additive-only within v1**: new optional fields,
new `kind` variants, new ops may appear at any time; existing
spellings never change meaning. Every consumer obligation follows:

* Renderers meeting an unknown `kind` degrade to generic KV.
* `props` is an open map — renderers ignore keys they don't know.
* `contributes.extra` round-trips unknown chrome slots.
* Plugin `render` failures fall back to built-in interpretation.

A driver written today keeps working as the IR grows; a renderer
written today keeps working as drivers grow. Forward compatibility
is mandatory, not optional — it's what makes "install a driver,
get visualization everywhere" true across versions.

## Data binding, not data copying

Nodes don't embed data — they name a `query` binding, and the host
resolves bindings to view-model data before rendering (cached,
with partial degradation per binding). Drivers declare *what* data
a view needs; hosts decide *when* to fetch it. That split is what
lets `pavo view --param` and deep-link params flow through one
mechanism, and lets the web surface hydrate panels independently.

## Escape hatches where they belong

Declarative doesn't mean lowest-common-denominator. `embed` names a
component for rich visuals; `renderers[]` + the `render` op let a
driver claim a whole kind and answer with a canonical
`RenderModel`; `graph`'s IR floor covers structure while layout is
explicitly the renderer's problem. The IR covers the 90%; plugins
cover the 10% — and fallback is mandatory so plugins can fail
softly. See [Renderer plugins](/explanation/renderer-plugins).

## The cost

Honest trade-offs: the IR can't express everything (rich
interaction beyond single-form submit — buttons, wizards — is v2),
renderer plugins add a second contract to keep
honest, and every driver pays the manifest+wire ceremony even for a
trivial view. The bet is that uniform surfaces + safe degradation
outweigh per-product UI silos — the same bet the org's other tools
(sturn's WAL, tamias's ref grammar, cuora's refs) already make.

---

---
url: /pavo/explanation/renderer-plugins.md
---
# Renderer plugins

Built-in rendering is the floor, not the ceiling. A driver can ship
a **renderer plugin** — a claim on ViewNode *kinds* plus a `render`
op that returns a canonical `RenderModel` — and pavo routes matching
nodes to it instead of interpreting them natively.

There is no separate plugin ecosystem: plugins are tamias drivers.
`examples/drivers/viz-graph/` claims `graph` on all three surfaces
and renders SVG/ascii the built-ins don't; its manifest declares
**zero views** — it renders other drivers' trees.

## The two halves

**Manifest half** — `renderers[]` declares the claim:

```json
{"id": "graph", "kinds": ["graph"], "priority": 50,
 "surfaces": {
   "cli": {"formats": ["svg", "ascii"]},
   "tui": true,
   "web": {"component": "viz-graph", "island": true}}}
```

`kinds` lists ViewNode kinds (or `"*"` for catch-all); `surfaces`
says where the claim holds and which `--format` values it takes
(empty `formats` = wildcard). Absent surface = unsupported there.

**Wire half** — the `render` op:

```
→ {"op":"render","kind":"graph","node":{…ViewNode verbatim…},
   "data":{…view bindings…},"surface":"cli","format":"svg"}
← {"ok":true,"result":{"type":"svg","markup":"<svg>…"}}
```

`node` arrives untyped so unknown/future fields survive;
`data` is the same binding map `view` returns, so the plugin
resolves `node.query` itself.

## Claim resolution

Deterministic, same policy as chrome contributions:

1. Explicit kinds beat `"*"`.
2. Lower `priority` wins (default 100).
3. Ties break by driver name, then renderer id.

`pavo`'s `RendererRegistry` (pavo-core `renderers` module) folds
all manifests into this order once at discovery; `/api/renderers`
on `pavo serve` exposes the resolved claims to the web surface.

## Precedence over built-ins

Plugin claims are **canonical per node** on every surface: a node
whose kind+surface is claimed renders via `render` → RenderModel;
built-ins are the fallback for unclaimed kinds *and* for plugin
failures. On `cli` this includes `--format` names that collide with
built-ins — `text`, `dot`, and `mermaid` are claimable via
`cli.formats` (empty = wildcard), and a claim wins for the nodes it
covers while unclaimed nodes keep the built-in output. `json` is the
one exception: the raw `ViewResult` dump is host-owned and never
routed to plugins. On `web` the same rule makes the plugin
RenderModel canonical for claimed kinds — `GraphIsland.vue` is the
`graph` fallback when no plugin claims it (and while the render op
is in flight a placeholder shows, never the built-in).

## RenderModel — the canonical output

Plugins don't ship surface code; they answer one of four tagged
models and each surface maps it natively:

| variant | CLI | TUI | web |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `rows` | aligned table | table rows | `<table>` |
| `svg` | raw markup | `[svg]` hint | `v-html` island |
| `text` | lines | lines | `<pre>` |
| `placeholder` | `[component]` | box + detail | named component |

The set is deliberately small — plugins needing richer output use
`placeholder` (web components) or `svg` (self-contained markup).
**No HTML in RenderModel**: self-contained markup is `svg` only.

## The fallback contract

* **Built-ins are not reserved.** A plugin may claim `graph` (or
  any kind) and override built-in rendering on the surfaces it
  declares.
* **Fallback is mandatory.** When no plugin claims a kind+surface,
  or `render` errors/times out, hosts use the built-in
  interpretation — unknown kinds still degrade to KV. Plugin failure
  must never break a view; that's what makes plugins safe to
  discover on `PATH` alongside everything else.
* **`web.component` is a hint.** v1 renders every RenderModel
  generically; `component`/`island` name rich mounts for hosts that
  resolve them (dynamic-imported components are a v2 concern).

## Why plugins instead of `embed`

`embed` names a component for *one node*; a renderer plugin claims
a *kind* — every `graph` node in every view, from every driver.
Plugins are how `graph` itself migrated: the IR keeps the
structure, the plugin owns the rendering. `table`/`list` plugins
are the expected next migrations.

---

---
url: /pavo/explanation/boundaries.md
---
# Boundaries

Pavo owns **visualization hosting** — driver discovery, ViewNode
interpretation, contribution-slot merge, renderer-plugin dispatch,
and the three renderers (CLI, TUI, web). Neighbors own theirs:

* **tamias** — distribution. Drivers are tamias content packages:
  executables named `tamias-driver-<type>` found on `PATH` or in
  `<tamias-home>/drivers/`. Pavo never re-implements transport or
  content types; it only *executes* what tamias installed.
* **products** (myco, kuda, sturn, mimus, cuora, …) — state owners.
  They ship drivers that proxy their existing `serve` wires (see
  the [proxy pattern](/how-to/write-a-driver#the-proxy-pattern-recommended-for-real-products)).
  Pavo never reads product internals — no myco files, no kuda
  sqlite, no store schemas. If a driver needs product state, the
  product's own `serve` is the API.
* **cuora** — secrets. Driver credentials via `cuora://` refs;
  pavo never sees values.
* **rampho** — the `SceneNode → ViewNode` precedent: media render
  pipelines are rampho's, UI trees are pavo's.
* **peregrin** — orchestration. Multi-actor concerns (who may view
  what, from where) are policy; pavo serves one localhost user.
  Note: peregrin's `tamias-driver-peregrin` is a tamias *content*
  driver for bundle install/deploy — it does not yet serve pavo
  views.
* **sepia** — session lifecycle; unrelated to rendering.

## What pavo deliberately doesn't do

* **No plugin system beyond drivers.** "Files, not frameworks" —
  a driver is an executable on `PATH`; renderer plugins are the
  same mechanism with a `renderers[]` manifest claim.
* **No product semantics.** ViewNode kinds are generic
  (`table`, not `issue-list`); meaning lives in the driver's
  queries and labels. The config API is namespaced dotted keys,
  never file paths.
* **No host-side writes.** `form` nodes submit through the
  driver's own `submit` wire op — pavo hosts collect field values
  and display the `SubmitResult`, but every mutation semantic
  (what `submit_op` means, what gets written) belongs to the
  driver. Drivers stay proxies; pavo never touches product state.
* **No daemon.** `pavo serve` is a per-user localhost bridge bound
  to `127.0.0.1`, not a service. Multi-user or remote hosting
  would be a different tool.
* **No HTML from drivers.** The IR is declarative; `svg` is the
  only self-contained markup a plugin may emit. Anything richer is
  `placeholder`/`embed` resolved host-side.
